title: Actual parameter
body:
What the caller actually passes at the **call site**. Also called the *argument*.

```c++
int x = 2, y = 3;
cout << add(x, y);      // x and y are the actual parameters
cout << add(2, 3);      // so are these
cout << add(x + 1, 3);  // and this expression
```

Unlike a [[Formal parameter]], an actual parameter does not have to be a variable. Literals,
expressions, and the return values of other function calls all work, because all the function
needs is a value to copy. See [[Call by value]].

**Unless it is a reference parameter.** `void f(int& n)` needs somewhere to write back to, so
the actual parameter has to be a variable and `f(x + 1)` is a
[[Compile Errors|compile error]]. That is the rule stated in [[Call by reference]], and this is
where it comes from.

Actuals bind to formals **by position**, left to right, and the types have to be compatible
(or implicitly convertible; see [[Type casting]]). Nothing checks that the *meaning* lines up,
so `divide(denominator, numerator)` compiles perfectly and is wrong.
